title: How A Simple Change In Thinking Can Improve Behavior ve-behavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In this short, focused piece, Linsin argues that difficult students often misbehave because teachers unconsciously expect them to, and that expectation itself becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy through subtle verbal and nonverbal cues. His prescribed fix is a deliberate internal reframe: assume the most challenging students will behave well, treating them as trustworthy and independent as any other student, without becoming lax on genuine supervision or accountability. He explains that this shift removes the accumulated negative signals—tone, body language, anticipatory tension—that reinforce a student's poor self-image and defiance. The piece closes with an emotionally charged description of this reframe helping students see and grow into a better version of themselves that they may not have believed possible.
points: Teacher expectations of misbehavior function as a self-fulfilling prophecy for difficult students.
The prescribed fix is a deliberate internal reframe: assume difficult students will behave well, without lowering actual supervision or accountability standards.
This reframe removes subtle verbal and nonverbal cues that unintentionally signal distrust or resentment.
The shift can transform a student's attitude from believing the teacher is 'out to get them' to seeing the teacher as an ally.
The approach aims to help students grow into a positive version of themselves they may not have believed was possible.
quotes: One of the reasons difficult students misbehave is because their teacher expects that they will.
To combat this phenomenon, you must do the opposite. You must assume henceforth that your most challenging students will, of their own accord, behave . . . perfectly.
That isn’t to say that you’ll become lax in your supervision, ignore their misbehavior, or in any way become less consistent holding them accountable.
This simple change in thinking—in how you choose to see them—effectively removes an infinite number of verbal and non-verbal signals that reinforce their poor behavior.
It upends their attitude toward you, transforming them from someone who firmly believes that you’re out to get them . . . into your biggest fan.
They’ll see in your eyes a reflection of themselves they may not at first recognize, but who deep down they’ve always wanted to be.
